claim: bioBakery 3 is a set of integrated, improved methods for taxonomic, strain-level, functional, and phylogenetic profiling of metagenomes.
source: To leverage these, we present bioBakery 3, a set of integrated, improved methods for taxonomic, strain-level, functional, and phylogenetic profiling of metagenomes newly developed to build on the largest set of reference sequences now available.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the platform being presented.

claim: MetaPhlAn 3 increases the accuracy of taxonomic profiling compared to current alternatives.
source: Compared to current alternatives, MetaPhlAn 3 increases the accuracy of taxonomic profiling, and HUMAnN 3 improves that of functional potential and activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative evaluations presented in the manuscript showing improved performance metrics.

claim: HUMAnN 3 improves the accuracy of functional potential and activity profiling.
source: Compared to current alternatives, MetaPhlAn 3 increases the accuracy of taxonomic profiling, and HUMAnN 3 improves that of functional potential and activity.
evidence: This is supported by benchmark data comparing HUMAnN 3 to HUMAnN 2 and Carnelian.

claim: bioBakery 3 methods detected novel disease-microbiome links in applications to CRC with 1262 metagenomes.
source: These methods detected novel disease-microbiome links in applications to CRC (1262 metagenomes) and IBD (1635 metagenomes and 817 metatranscriptomes).
evidence: This is supported by the meta-analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: bioBakery 3 methods detected novel disease-microbiome links in applications to IBD with 1635 metagenomes and 817 metatranscriptomes.
source: These methods detected novel disease-microbiome links in applications to CRC (1262 metagenomes) and IBD (1635 metagenomes and 817 metatranscriptomes).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of the HMP2 IBD dataset.

claim: StrainPhlAn 3 and PanPhlAn 3 profiled 4077 metagenomes to unravel the phylogenetic and functional structure of Ruminococcus bromii.
source: Strain-level profiling of an additional 4077 metagenomes with StrainPhlAn 3 and PanPhlAn 3 unraveled the phylogenetic and functional structure of the common gut microbe Ruminococcus bromii, previously described by only 15 isolate genomes.
evidence: This is supported by the detailed analysis of R. bromii presented in the results section.

claim: Ruminococcus bromii was previously described by only 15 isolate genomes.
source: Strain-level profiling of an additional 4077 metagenomes with StrainPhlAn 3 and PanPhlAn 3 unraveled the phylogenetic and functional structure of the common gut microbe Ruminococcus bromii, previously described by only 15 isolate genomes.
evidence: This is stated as background information about the limited prior genomic characterization of this species.

claim: ChocoPhlAn 3 is based on 99.2k high-quality, fully annotated reference microbial genomes from 16.8k species.
source: ChocoPhlAn 3 is based on a genomic repository of 99.2 k high-quality, fully annotated reference microbial genomes from 16.8 k species available in the UniProt Proteomes portal as of January 2019 (The UniProt Consortium, 2019) and the corresponding functionally-annotated 87.3M UniRef90 gene families (Suzek et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the data sources used to build the ChocoPhlAn 3 database.

claim: ChocoPhlAn 3 includes 87.3M functionally-annotated UniRef90 gene families.
source: ChocoPhlAn 3 is based on a genomic repository of 99.2 k high-quality, fully annotated reference microbial genomes from 16.8 k species available in the UniProt Proteomes portal as of January 2019 (The UniProt Consortium, 2019) and the corresponding functionally-annotated 87.3M UniRef90 gene families (Suzek et al., 2015).
evidence: This quantifies the gene family content of the ChocoPhlAn 3 database.

claim: MetaPhlAn 3 incorporates 13.5k species, more than twice as many as MetaPhlAn 2.
source: MetaPhlAn 3 incorporates 13.5 k species (more than twice as much as MetaPhlAn 2) with a completely new set of 1.1M marker genes (84 ± 47 mean ± SD markers per species) selected by ChocoPhlAn 3 from the set of 16.8 k species pangenomes.
evidence: This quantifies the expansion of species coverage in MetaPhlAn 3.

claim: MetaPhlAn 3 uses 1.1M marker genes with 84 ± 47 mean ± SD markers per species.
source: MetaPhlAn 3 incorporates 13.5 k species (more than twice as much as MetaPhlAn 2) with a completely new set of 1.1M marker genes (84 ± 47 mean ± SD markers per species) selected by ChocoPhlAn 3 from the set of 16.8 k species pangenomes.
evidence: This describes the marker gene database used by MetaPhlAn 3.

claim: MetaPhlAn 3 outperformed all other profilers across all considered types of communities when assessing the F1 score.
source: MetaPhlAn 3 outperformed all the other profilers across all considered types of communities when assessing the F1 score (Figure 1B), which is a measure combining the fraction of species actually present in the metagenomes that are correctly detected (recall, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and the fraction of species predicted to be present that were actually included in the synthetic metagenome (precision, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by benchmark results shown in Figure 1B comparing MetaPhlAn 3 to other tools.

claim: MetaPhlAn 3 had an average of 8.51 ± 5.12 false positive species detected.
source: With a very low number of false positive species detected, MetaPhlAn 3 (avg 8.51 s.d. 5.12) also maximized precision (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) with respect to the other tools (avg 9 s.d. 4.78 for mOTUs2 in high precision mode, the closest competitor on precision).
evidence: This quantifies the false positive rate of MetaPhlAn 3 in the benchmark.

claim: mOTUs2 in high precision mode had an average of 9 ± 4.78 false positive species detected.
source: With a very low number of false positive species detected, MetaPhlAn 3 (avg 8.51 s.d. 5.12) also maximized precision (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) with respect to the other tools (avg 9 s.d. 4.78 for mOTUs2 in high precision mode, the closest competitor on precision).
evidence: This quantifies the false positive rate of mOTUs2 in the benchmark.

claim: Bracken had on average 729 false positive species across the synthetic metagenomes.
source: On recall, Bracken and mOTUs2 in high-recall mode were in several cases superior to MetaPhlAn 3, but at the cost of a very high number of false positives (on average 729 species for Bracken and 39 for mOTUs2 high-recall, for a total of 86,077 and 4655 false positive species across the synthetic metagenomes).
evidence: This quantifies the high false positive rate of Bracken.

claim: mOTUs2 in high-recall mode had on average 39 false positive species across the synthetic metagenomes.
source: On recall, Bracken and mOTUs2 in high-recall mode were in several cases superior to MetaPhlAn 3, but at the cost of a very high number of false positives (on average 729 species for Bracken and 39 for mOTUs2 high-recall, for a total of 86,077 and 4655 false positive species across the synthetic metagenomes).
evidence: This quantifies the false positive rate of mOTUs2 in high-recall mode.

claim: 379 of the total 1119 species (33%) in the synthetic metagenomes were not present in the MetaPhlAn 2 database.
source: Of note, 379 of the total 1119 (33%) species in the synthetic metagenomes were not present in the database of MetaPhlAn 2, emphasizing the role of expanded isolate genome availability in the improved detection capabilities of MetaPhlAn 3.
evidence: This quantifies the database expansion benefit for species detection.

claim: MetaPhlAn 3 is more than 3 times faster than MetaPhlAn 2.
source: It is >3 x faster than MetaPhlAn 2 (10.0k vs. 2.9 k reads/s on a Xeon Gold 6140) and almost matches the speed of Bracken (11 k reads/s).
evidence: This is based on performance benchmarking data.

claim: MetaPhlAn 3 processes 10.0k reads/s on a Xeon Gold 6140.
source: It is >3 x faster than MetaPhlAn 2 (10.0k vs. 2.9 k reads/s on a Xeon Gold 6140) and almost matches the speed of Bracken (11 k reads/s).
evidence: This quantifies the processing speed of MetaPhlAn 3.

claim: MetaPhlAn 2 processes 2.9k reads/s on a Xeon Gold 6140.
source: It is >3 x faster than MetaPhlAn 2 (10.0k vs. 2.9 k reads/s on a Xeon Gold 6140) and almost matches the speed of Bracken (11 k reads/s).
evidence: This quantifies the processing speed of MetaPhlAn 2.

claim: Bracken processes 11k reads/s.
source: It is >3 x faster than MetaPhlAn 2 (10.0k vs. 2.9 k reads/s on a Xeon Gold 6140) and almost matches the speed of Bracken (11 k reads/s).
evidence: This quantifies the processing speed of Bracken.

claim: MetaPhlAn 3 memory usage is 2.6 Gb for a complete taxonomic profiling run.
source: MetaPhlAn 3 memory usage is slightly higher (2.6 Gb for a complete taxonomic profiling run) than MetaPhlAn 2 (2.1Gb), but outperforms the other methods (4.3 Gb for mOTUs2 and 32.5 Gb for Bracken, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This quantifies the memory requirements of MetaPhlAn 3.

claim: MetaPhlAn 2 memory usage is 2.1 Gb.
source: MetaPhlAn 3 memory usage is slightly higher (2.6 Gb for a complete taxonomic profiling run) than MetaPhlAn 2 (2.1Gb), but outperforms the other methods (4.3 Gb for mOTUs2 and 32.5 Gb for Bracken, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This quantifies the memory requirements of MetaPhlAn 2.

claim: mOTUs2 memory usage is 4.3 Gb.
source: MetaPhlAn 3 memory usage is slightly higher (2.6 Gb for a complete taxonomic profiling run) than MetaPhlAn 2 (2.1Gb), but outperforms the other methods (4.3 Gb for mOTUs2 and 32.5 Gb for Bracken, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This quantifies the memory requirements of mOTUs2.

claim: Bracken memory usage is 32.5 Gb.
source: MetaPhlAn 3 memory usage is slightly higher (2.6 Gb for a complete taxonomic profiling run) than MetaPhlAn 2 (2.1Gb), but outperforms the other methods (4.3 Gb for mOTUs2 and 32.5 Gb for Bracken, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This quantifies the memory requirements of Bracken.

claim: HUMAnN 3 produced highly accurate estimates of community-level EC abundances across the 30 CAMI metagenomes with mean ± SD of Bray-Curtis similarity = 0.93 ± 0.03.
source: HUMAnN 3 produced highly accurate estimates of community-level EC abundances across the 30 CAMI metagenomes (mean ± SD of Bray-Curtis similarity = 0.93 ± 0.03, Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on benchmark comparisons against gold standard functional profiles.

claim: HUMAnN 2 achieved community-level EC abundance accuracy of 0.70 ± 0.04 Bray-Curtis similarity.
source: HUMAnN 2 followed with an accuracy of 0.70 ± 0.04 and Carnelian at 0.49 ± 0.04.
evidence: This quantifies HUMAnN 2 performance in the benchmark.

claim: Carnelian achieved community-level EC abundance accuracy of 0.49 ± 0.04 Bray-Curtis similarity.
source: HUMAnN 2 followed with an accuracy of 0.70 ± 0.04 and Carnelian at 0.49 ± 0.04.
evidence: This quantifies Carnelian performance in the benchmark.

claim: HUMAnN 3 exhibited the highest sensitivity (0.96 ± 0.05) for EC detection.
source: HUMAnN 3 exhibited the highest sensitivity (0.96 ± 0.05), while HUMAnN 2 and Carnelian had similar lower sensitivity scores (0.72 ± 0.05 and 0.74 ± 0.04, respectively).
evidence: This is based on F1 score analysis of EC detection.

claim: HUMAnN 2 had sensitivity of 0.72 ± 0.05 for EC detection.
source: HUMAnN 3 exhibited the highest sensitivity (0.96 ± 0.05), while HUMAnN 2 and Carnelian had similar lower sensitivity scores (0.72 ± 0.05 and 0.74 ± 0.04, respectively).
evidence: This quantifies HUMAnN 2 sensitivity in the benchmark.

claim: Carnelian had sensitivity of 0.74 ± 0.04 for EC detection.
source: HUMAnN 3 exhibited the highest sensitivity (0.96 ± 0.05), while HUMAnN 2 and Carnelian had similar lower sensitivity scores (0.72 ± 0.05 and 0.74 ± 0.04, respectively).
evidence: This quantifies Carnelian sensitivity in the benchmark.

claim: HUMAnN 3 had precision of 0.97 ± 0.01 for EC detection.
source: In contrast, HUMAnN 3 and HUMAnN 2 had similar high precision scores (0.97 ± 0.01 and 0.95 ± 0.02), while Carnelian's precision was uniquely lower (0.60 ± 0.08).
evidence: This quantifies HUMAnN 3 precision in the benchmark.

claim: HUMAnN 2 had precision of 0.95 ± 0.02 for EC detection.
source: In contrast, HUMAnN 3 and HUMAnN 2 had similar high precision scores (0.97 ± 0.01 and 0.95 ± 0.02), while Carnelian's precision was uniquely lower (0.60 ± 0.08).
evidence: This quantifies HUMAnN 2 precision in the benchmark.

claim: Carnelian had precision of 0.60 ± 0.08 for EC detection.
source: In contrast, HUMAnN 3 and HUMAnN 2 had similar high precision scores (0.97 ± 0.01 and 0.95 ± 0.02), while Carnelian's precision was uniquely lower (0.60 ± 0.08).
evidence: This quantifies Carnelian precision in the benchmark.

claim: EC accuracy for species with at least 1x mean coverage depth was 0.81 ± 0.16 for HUMAnN 3.
source: Across the CAMI metagenomes, EC accuracy for species with at least 1x mean coverage depth was 0.81 ± 0.16 for HUMAnN 3 and 0.51 ± 0.15 for HUMAnN 2 (mean ± SD within-species Bray-Curtis similarity; Figure 1).
evidence: This quantifies per-species functional profiling accuracy.

claim: EC accuracy for species with at least 1x mean coverage depth was 0.51 ± 0.15 for HUMAnN 2.
source: Across the CAMI metagenomes, EC accuracy for species with at least 1x mean coverage depth was 0.81 ± 0.16 for HUMAnN 3 and 0.51 ± 0.15 for HUMAnN 2 (mean ± SD within-species Bray-Curtis similarity; Figure 1).
evidence: This quantifies per-species functional profiling accuracy for HUMAnN 2.

claim: Carnelian analyzed the CAMI metagenomes in 26.4 ± 2.7 CPU-hours per sample.
source: Carnelian was the most computationally efficient of the three methods, analyzing the CAMI metagenomes in 26.4 ± 2.7 CPU-hours (per-sample mean ± SD) compared with 38.1 ± 12.8 CPU-hours for HUMAnN 2 and 52.5 ± 19.2 CPU-hours for HUMAnN 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This quantifies computational efficiency of Carnelian.

claim: HUMAnN 2 analyzed the CAMI metagenomes in 38.1 ± 12.8 CPU-hours per sample.
source: Carnelian was the most computationally efficient of the three methods, analyzing the CAMI metagenomes in 26.4 ± 2.7 CPU-hours (per-sample mean ± SD) compared with 38.1 ± 12.8 CPU-hours for HUMAnN 2 and 52.5 ± 19.2 CPU-hours for HUMAnN 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This quantifies computational efficiency of HUMAnN 2.

claim: HUMAnN 3 analyzed the CAMI metagenomes in 52.5 ± 19.2 CPU-hours per sample.
source: Carnelian was the most computationally efficient of the three methods, analyzing the CAMI metagenomes in 26.4 ± 2.7 CPU-hours (per-sample mean ± SD) compared with 38.1 ± 12.8 CPU-hours for HUMAnN 2 and 52.5 ± 19.2 CPU-hours for HUMAnN 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This quantifies computational efficiency of HUMAnN 3.

claim: Carnelian required 11.9 ± 0.0 GB peak memory use.
source: Trends in peak memory use (MaxRSS) were similar, with Carnelian requiring 11.9 ± 0.0 GB versus HUMAnN 2's 17.0 ± 0.3 GB and HUMAnN 3's 21.5 ± 1.9 GB.
evidence: This quantifies memory requirements of Carnelian.

claim: HUMAnN 2 required 17.0 ± 0.3 GB peak memory use.
source: Trends in peak memory use (MaxRSS) were similar, with Carnelian requiring 11.9 ± 0.0 GB versus HUMAnN 2's 17.0 ± 0.3 GB and HUMAnN 3's 21.5 ± 1.9 GB.
evidence: This quantifies memory requirements of HUMAnN 2.

claim: HUMAnN 3 required 21.5 ± 1.9 GB peak memory use.
source: Trends in peak memory use (MaxRSS) were similar, with Carnelian requiring 11.9 ± 0.0 GB versus HUMAnN 2's 17.0 ± 0.3 GB and HUMAnN 3's 21.5 ± 1.9 GB.
evidence: This quantifies memory requirements of HUMAnN 3.

claim: The CRC meta-analysis included 1262 samples from nine different datasets spanning eight different countries.
source: To illustrate the potential of bioBakery 3's updated profiling tools and to extend our understanding of the microbial signatures in colorectal cancer (CRC), we expanded our previous work to meta-analyze both existing and newly available CRC metagenomic cohorts for a total of 1262 samples (600 control and 662 CRC samples) from nine different datasets spanning eight different countries (Feng et al., 2015; Gupta et al., 2019; Thomas et al., 2019; Vogtmann et al., 2016; Wirbel et al., 2019; Yachida et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2017; Zeller et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the scope of the CRC meta-analysis.

claim: The CRC meta-analysis included 600 control samples and 662 CRC samples.
source: To illustrate the potential of bioBakery 3's updated profiling tools and to extend our understanding of the microbial signatures in colorectal cancer (CRC), we expanded our previous work to meta-analyze both existing and newly available CRC metagenomic cohorts for a total of 1262 samples (600 control and 662 CRC samples) from nine different datasets spanning eight different countries (Feng et al., 2015; Gupta et al., 2019; Thomas et al., 2019; Vogtmann et al., 2016; Wirbel et al., 2019; Yachida et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2017; Zeller et al., 2014).
evidence: This quantifies the sample composition of the CRC meta-analysis.

claim: MetaPhlAn 3 identified a total of 1083 species detected at least once in the CRC meta-analysis.
source: MetaPhlAn 3 identified a total of 1083 species detected at least once (172 considered 'prevalent' when defined as present in >5% of samples at >0.1% relative abundance), of which 505 species (52 prevalent) were previously not reported by MetaPhlAn 2 due to the expansion of the genome database (or in some cases because of changes in the NCBI taxonomy).
evidence: This quantifies the species detected in the CRC meta-analysis.

claim: 172 species were considered prevalent in the CRC meta-analysis (present in >5% of samples at >0.1% relative abundance).
source: MetaPhlAn 3 identified a total of 1083 species detected at least once (172 considered 'prevalent' when defined as present in >5% of samples at >0.1% relative abundance), of which 505 species (52 prevalent) were previously not reported by MetaPhlAn 2 due to the expansion of the genome database (or in some cases because of changes in the NCBI taxonomy).
evidence: This defines and quantifies prevalent species in the CRC analysis.

claim: 505 species detected by MetaPhlAn 3 in the CRC meta-analysis were previously not reported by MetaPhlAn 2.
source: MetaPhlAn 3 identified a total of 1083 species detected at least once (172 considered 'prevalent' when defined as present in >5% of samples at >0.1% relative abundance), of which 505 species (52 prevalent) were previously not reported by MetaPhlAn 2 due to the expansion of the genome database (or in some cases because of changes in the NCBI taxonomy).
evidence: This quantifies the new species detected by MetaPhlAn 3.

claim: 82 species present in the MetaPhlAn 2 database were not detected by MetaPhlAn 2 but are now identified by MetaPhlAn 3.
source: In addition, 82 species present in the MetaPhlAn 2 database were not detected by MetaPhlAn 2 but are now identified in the samples by MetaPhlAn 3, due to the expanded sequence catalog, improved marker discovery procedure, and increased sensitivity to low-abundance species (Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: This quantifies improved detection of previously missed species.

claim: 121 species were significantly associated with CRC (FDR q < 0.05 and Q-test for heterogeneity >0.05).
source: We found 121 species significantly associated with CRC (FDR q < 0.05 and Q-test for heterogeneity >0.05; Supplementary file 6) by a meta-analysis of standardized mean differences using a random-effects model on arcsine-square-root-transformed relative abundances (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This quantifies the CRC-associated species identified.

claim: 60 additional species reached significance in the CRC meta-analysis compared to MetaPhlAn 2.
source: Compared to MetaPhlAn 2 when run on the same data, this includes 60 additional species that reached significance in the meta-analysis, confirming that the updated methods lead to improved biomarker discovery.
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in biomarker discovery.

claim: Dialister pneumosintes, Ruthenibacterium lactatiformans, and Eisenbergiella tayi are three additional species strongly associated with CRC (effect size >0.35) not identified in previous MetaPhlAn-2-based analysis.
source: Among them, three additional species not identified in previous MetaPhlAn-2-based analysis (Thomas et al., 2019) were among those most strongly associated with CRC (effect size >0.35): Dialister pneumosintes, Ruthenibacterium lactatiformans, and Eisenbergiella tayi (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This identifies novel CRC-associated species discovered with MetaPhlAn 3.

claim: Dialister pneumosintes is typically oral.
source: Dialister pneumosintes is typically oral, further reinforcing the role of oral taxa in CRC, and R. lactatiformans was reported as part of a consortium of bacteria able to increase colonic IFNγ+T cells (Tanoue et al., 2019).
evidence: This provides biological context for one of the newly identified CRC-associated species.

claim: R. lactatiformans was reported as part of a consortium of bacteria able to increase colonic IFNγ+T cells.
source: Dialister pneumosintes is typically oral, further reinforcing the role of oral taxa in CRC, and R. lactatiformans was reported as part of a consortium of bacteria able to increase colonic IFNγ+T cells (Tanoue et al., 2019).
evidence: This provides biological context from prior literature.

claim: HUMAnN 3 identified 4.3M UniRef90 gene families in the CRC meta-analysis.
source: Functional profiling of this expanded CRC meta-analysis with HUMAnN 3 identified 4.3M UniRef90 gene families, corresponding to 549 MetaCyc pathways and 2895 ECs.
evidence: This quantifies the functional features detected in the CRC analysis.

claim: HUMAnN 3 identified 549 MetaCyc pathways in the CRC meta-analysis.
source: Functional profiling of this expanded CRC meta-analysis with HUMAnN 3 identified 4.3M UniRef90 gene families, corresponding to 549 MetaCyc pathways and 2895 ECs.
evidence: This quantifies the pathways detected in the CRC analysis.

claim: HUMAnN 3 identified 2895 ECs in the CRC meta-analysis.
source: Functional profiling of this expanded CRC meta-analysis with HUMAnN 3 identified 4.3M UniRef90 gene families, corresponding to 549 MetaCyc pathways and 2895 ECs.
evidence: This quantifies the enzyme families detected in the CRC analysis.

claim: 206,296 gene families were significantly associated with CRC and controls (FDR q < 0.05).
source: Out of these 4.3M gene families, the meta-analysis identified 206,296 significantly associated with CRC and controls (FDR q < 0.05), a substantial increase from the 64,315 gene families previously identified with the meta-analysis based on HUMAnN 2 profiles (FDR q < 0.05).
evidence: This quantifies the CRC-associated gene families identified.

claim: 64,315 gene families were previously identified as CRC-associated with HUMAnN 2 profiles (FDR q < 0.05).
source: Out of these 4.3M gene families, the meta-analysis identified 206,296 significantly associated with CRC and controls (FDR q < 0.05), a substantial increase from the 64,315 gene families previously identified with the meta-analysis based on HUMAnN 2 profiles (FDR q < 0.05).
evidence: This provides comparison to previous analysis results.

claim: 120 MetaCyc pathways were significantly associated with CRC (Wilcoxon rank-sum test FDR q < 0.05 and Q-test for heterogeneity >0.05).
source: In addition, 120 MetaCyc pathways were significantly associated with CRC (Wilcoxon rank-sum test FDR q < 0.05 and Q-test for heterogeneity >0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), of which 59 (49.1%) overlapped previous results, including for example the increased abundance of starch degradation V (Supplementary file 6) in healthy individuals.
evidence: This quantifies the CRC-associated pathways identified.

claim: 59 (49.1%) of the CRC-associated pathways overlapped with previous results.
source: In addition, 120 MetaCyc pathways were significantly associated with CRC (Wilcoxon rank-sum test FDR q < 0.05 and Q-test for heterogeneity >0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), of which 59 (49.1%) overlapped previous results, including for example the increased abundance of starch degradation V (Supplementary file 6) in healthy individuals.
evidence: This quantifies the overlap with previous findings.

claim: Starch degradation V pathway showed increased abundance in healthy individuals.
source: In addition, 120 MetaCyc pathways were significantly associated with CRC (Wilcoxon rank-sum test FDR q < 0.05 and Q-test for heterogeneity >0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), of which 59 (49.1%) overlapped previous results, including for example the increased abundance of starch degradation V (Supplementary file 6) in healthy individuals.
evidence: This describes a specific pathway association with health status.

claim: Bifidobacterium breve and other Bifidobacterium spp encode amylopullulanases and attach to starch particles.
source: Bifidobacterium breve and other Bifidobacterium spp have been shown to encode amylopullulanases and attach to starch particles, and they have also been reported for their potential protective role against carcinogenesis here and previously (Sivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Bifidobacterium species have been reported for their potential protective role against carcinogenesis.
source: Bifidobacterium breve and other Bifidobacterium spp have been shown to encode amylopullulanases and attach to starch particles, and they have also been reported for their potential protective role against carcinogenesis here and previously (Sivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and current findings.

claim: HUMAnN 3 directly profiled relative abundances of 113 UniRef90 gene families annotated as cutC orthologs.
source: HUMAnN 3 was instead able to directly profile relative abundances of 113 UniRef90 gene families annotated as cutC orthologs and identified 909 metagenomes in this data collection carrying at least one gene family annotated as cutC.
evidence: This quantifies the cutC gene families profiled.

claim: 909 metagenomes in the CRC data collection carry at least one gene family annotated as cutC.
source: HUMAnN 3 was instead able to directly profile relative abundances of 113 UniRef90 gene families annotated as cutC orthologs and identified 909 metagenomes in this data collection carrying at least one gene family annotated as cutC.
evidence: This quantifies the prevalence of cutC in the dataset.

claim: cutC relative abundance is significantly increased in CRC samples compared to controls (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.05 in six of the nine datasets, meta-analysis p<0.0001).
source: These confirmed an increase of cutC relative abundance in CRC samples compared to controls (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.05 in six of the nine datasets, meta-analysis p<0.0001).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of cutC abundance.

claim: yeaW gene showed only weak associations with CRC disease status (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.05 in three of the nine datasets, meta-analysis p=0.095).
source: Interestingly, a meta-analysis performed on the relative abundances of the L-carnitine dioxygenase gene (yeaW), a gene also involved in trimethylamine synthesis, revealed only weak associations with disease status (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.05 in three of the nine datasets, meta-analysis p=0.095, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), possibly reflecting a stronger effect of dietary choline on CRC risk compared to carnitine.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of yeaW abundance.

claim: Random forest classification using MetaPhlAn 3 features achieved 0.85 average AUC for CRC sample classification in leave-one-dataset-out evaluations.
source: MetaPhlAn 3 and HUMAnN 3 also proved accurate when combining CRC microbiomes using more purely discriminative models such as random forests (RFs), reaching 0.85 average AUC for CRC (vs. control) sample classification in leave-one-dataset-out evaluations using taxonomic features (LODO, minimum 0.76 for the YachidaS_2019 and ThomasAM_2019_a datasets, maximum 0.97 for the GuptaA_2019 dataset; Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This quantifies the classification performance.

claim: Random forest classification using functional features achieved 0.69 cross validation and 0.71 LODO ROC AUC on pathways relative abundance.
source: As in previous studies (Pasolli et al., 2016; Thomas et al., 2019), RFs using functional features performed similarly (0.69 cross validation and 0.71 LODO ROC AUC on pathways relative abundance), indicating a tight link between strain-specific taxonomy and gene carriage in this setting.
evidence: This quantifies the classification performance using functional features.

claim: The HMP2 IBD cohort included 1635 shotgun metagenomes and 817 shotgun metatranscriptomes.
source: To further demonstrate the utility of MetaPhlAn 3 and HUMAnN 3 on combined meta-omic sequencing datasets, including identification of expression-level biomarkers, we applied the updated methods to 1635 shotgun metagenomes (MGX) and 817 shotgun metatranscriptomes (MTX) derived from the stool samples of the HMP2 Inflammatory Bowel Disease Multi-omics Database (IBDMDB) cohort (http://ibdmdb.org; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the dataset used for IBD analysis.

claim: MetaPhlAn 3 identified more species pangenomes than MetaPhlAn 2 in the HMP2 dataset (MGX medians 40 vs. 48, MTX medians 40 vs. 47).
source: Compared with previously published profiles of the samples generated with MetaPhlAn 2 and HUMAnN 2 (IBDMDB Investigators et al., 2019; Figure 3A), the v3 methods' profiles (i) identified more species pangenomes (MGX medians 40 vs. 48, MTX medians 40 vs. 47); (ii) explained larger fractions of sample reads by mapping to pangenomes (MGX medians 54 vs. 63%, MTX medians 12 vs. 22%); and (iii) explained larger total fractions of sample reads after falling back to translated search (MGX medians 69 vs. 75%, MTX medians 20 vs. 31%).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in species detection.

claim: HUMAnN 3 explained larger fractions of sample reads by mapping to pangenomes than HUMAnN 2 (MGX medians 54 vs. 63%, MTX medians 12 vs. 22%).
source: Compared with previously published profiles of the samples generated with MetaPhlAn 2 and HUMAnN 2 (IBDMDB Investigators et al., 2019; Figure 3A), the v3 methods' profiles (i) identified more species pangenomes (MGX medians 40 vs. 48, MTX medians 40 vs. 47); (ii) explained larger fractions of sample reads by mapping to pangenomes (MGX medians 54 vs. 63%, MTX medians 12 vs. 22%); and (iii) explained larger total fractions of sample reads after falling back to translated search (MGX medians 69 vs. 75%, MTX medians 20 vs. 31%).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in read mapping.

claim: HUMAnN 3 explained larger total fractions of sample reads after translated search than HUMAnN 2 (MGX medians 69 vs. 75%, MTX medians 20 vs. 31%).
source: Compared with previously published profiles of the samples generated with MetaPhlAn 2 and HUMAnN 2 (IBDMDB Investigators et al., 2019; Figure 3A), the v3 methods' profiles (i) identified more species pangenomes (MGX medians 40 vs. 48, MTX medians 40 vs. 47); (ii) explained larger fractions of sample reads by mapping to pangenomes (MGX medians 54 vs. 63%, MTX medians 12 vs. 22%); and (iii) explained larger total fractions of sample reads after falling back to translated search (MGX medians 69 vs. 75%, MTX medians 20 vs. 31%).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in total read explanation.

claim: More than 500 Enzyme Commission (EC) families were significantly differentially expressed in active CD relative to inactive CD.
source: We identified 558 ECs whose residual expression was significantly different (FDR q < 0.05) in active CD compared with inactive CD (Figure 3B): a 66% increase compared to an identical analysis incorporating EC abundance profiles generated by HUMAnN 2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This quantifies the differentially expressed enzymes in active CD.

claim: 558 ECs were significantly differentially expressed in active CD, a 66% increase compared to HUMAnN 2 analysis.
source: We identified 558 ECs whose residual expression was significantly different (FDR q < 0.05) in active CD compared with inactive CD (Figure 3B): a 66% increase compared to an identical analysis incorporating EC abundance profiles generated by HUMAnN 2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in biomarker detection.

claim: Only one EC was differentially expressed in active UC (protein O-GlcNAcase, EC 3.2.1.169).
source: We identified only one EC that was differentially expressed in active UC (protein O-GlcNAcase, EC 3.2.1.169).
evidence: This identifies the single UC-associated enzyme.

claim: All but one of the significantly differentially expressed ECs in active CD were over-expressed.
source: Of the >500 significantly differentially expressed ECs in active CD, all but one were 'over-expressed' (i.e. their residual expression after controlling for DNA copy number was higher than expected in active CD; see Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the directionality of expression changes.

claim: Galactonate dehydratase (EC 4.2.1.6) was the one under-expressed function in active CD.
source: The one notable example of an 'under-expressed' function was galactonate dehydratase (EC 4.2.1.6; Figure 3C).
evidence: This identifies the single under-expressed enzyme.

claim: Galactonate dehydratase was encoded and highly expressed by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in both control and inactive CD samples.
source: This enzyme was encoded and highly expressed by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in both control and inactive CD samples.
evidence: This describes the species-level contribution to enzyme expression.

claim: Galactonate dehydratase was metagenomically abundant in active CD (contributed primarily by Escherichia coli) but not highly expressed.
source: While galactonate dehydratase was still metagenomically abundant in active CD (where it was contributed primarily by Escherichia coli), it was not highly expressed under those conditions.
evidence: This describes the differential expression pattern of the enzyme.

claim: Glutamyl-tRNA reductase (EC 1.2.1.70) had the highest novelty score (s = 0.46) among over-expressed functions in active CD.
source: Conversely, the highest novelty score was observed for glutamyl-tRNA reductase (EC 1.2.1.70, s = 0.46), a highly-transcribed housekeeping gene that received large contributions from the 3.0-new species Roseburia faecis, Phascolarctobacterium faecium, and Ruminococcus bicirculans.
evidence: This identifies the enzyme with highest contribution from newly detected species.

claim: Glutamyl-tRNA reductase received large contributions from the 3.0-new species Roseburia faecis, Phascolarctobacterium faecium, and Ruminococcus bicirculans.
source: Conversely, the highest novelty score was observed for glutamyl-tRNA reductase (EC 1.2.1.70, s = 0.46), a highly-transcribed housekeeping gene that received large contributions from the 3.0-new species Roseburia faecis, Phascolarctobacterium faecium, and Ruminococcus bicirculans.
evidence: This identifies the species contributing to this enzyme's expression.

claim: Betaine reductase (EC 1.21.4.4) had a novelty score of s = 0.43 and was contributed in part by Hungatella hathewayi.
source: Betaine reductase (EC 1.21.4.4, s = 0.43), instead, is much more specific and was contributed in part by 3.0-new species Hungatella hathewayi; this is notable as a rare example of a function that was often detectable from community RNA but not DNA (indicating high expression from a small pool of gene copies).
evidence: This describes a specific enzyme with high expression relative to gene copy number.

claim: Betaine reductase is a rare example of a function often detectable from community RNA but not DNA.
source: Betaine reductase (EC 1.21.4.4, s = 0.43), instead, is much more specific and was contributed in part by 3.0-new species Hungatella hathewayi; this is notable as a rare example of a function that was often detectable from community RNA but not DNA (indicating high expression from a small pool of gene copies).
evidence: This describes an unusual expression pattern.

claim: 4077 metagenomes containing Ruminococcus bromii were analyzed with StrainPhlAn 3 and PanPhlAn 3.
source: From the meta-analysis of 7783 gut metagenomes integrated for a previous study (Pasolli et al., 2019), we considered the 4077 metagenomes in which R. bromii was found present with a relative abundance above 0.05% according to MetaPhlAn 3.
evidence: This describes the dataset used for R. bromii analysis.

claim: StrainPhlAn analysis was based on single-nucleotide variants of 124 R. bromii-specific marker genes across 3375 samples.
source: StrainPhlAn analysis based on single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) of the 124 R. bromii-specific marker genes across the 3375 samples with sufficient markers' coverage (see Materials and methods) revealed a complex population structure not previously recapitulated by the only 15 genomes available from isolate sequencing (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the methodology and sample size for strain analysis.

claim: Two divergent sub-species clades of R. bromii were identified, with Cluster 1 mainly composed of strains from Chinese subjects and cohorts with rural and pre-industrial traditional lifestyle (Fisher's exact test p<2.2e-16).
source: Sub-clade prediction (see Materials and methods) highlighted two sub-species clades that are particularly divergent within the phylogeny (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D); interestingly, the first one (Cluster 1) is mainly composed of strains retrieved from Chinese subjects and from cohorts with a rural and a more pre-industrial traditional lifestyle and diet (Pasolli et al., 2019; Figure 4A; Cluster 1; Fisher's exact test p<2.2e-16).
evidence: This describes the geographic and lifestyle associations of R. bromii clades.

claim: StrainPhlAn 3 profiled 67.4% more strains than the previous version.
source: StrainPhlAn 3 can thus rapidly reconstruct complex strain-level phylogenies from metagenomes (5,700 s using 20 CPUs), and with the integration of PhyloPhlAn 3's improvements specifically for strain-level manipulation of alignments and phylogenies (Asnicar et al., 2020), surpasses the previous version of the software in accuracy and sensitivity (67.4% more strain profiled, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in strain profiling sensitivity.

claim: StrainPhlAn 3 can reconstruct complex strain-level phylogenies from metagenomes in 5,700 seconds using 20 CPUs.
source: StrainPhlAn 3 can thus rapidly reconstruct complex strain-level phylogenies from metagenomes (5,700 s using 20 CPUs), and with the integration of PhyloPhlAn 3's improvements specifically for strain-level manipulation of alignments and phylogenies (Asnicar et al., 2020), surpasses the previous version of the software in accuracy and sensitivity (67.4% more strain profiled, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This quantifies the computational efficiency of StrainPhlAn 3.

claim: Different individuals tend to carry different R. bromii strains with a mean normalized phylogenetic distance of 3.54e-3.
source: Specifically for R. bromii, different individuals tend to carry different strains diverged with a roughly normal distribution of genetic identities (mean 3.54e-3 normalized phylogenetic distance, Figure 4B).
evidence: This quantifies the inter-individual strain diversity.

claim: Genetic differences between R. bromii Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 had a mean normalized phylogenetic distance of 6.1e-3.
source: However, the genetic differences between Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 were generally greater, with a lower peak and higher distances (mean 6.1e-3, Figure 4B).
evidence: This quantifies the genetic divergence between major clades.

claim: 76.4% of within-subject R. bromii strain distances approached zero at distinct time points (average 261.35 ± 239.86 days).
source: For carriers of either clade, within-subject strain retention tended to be high as expected (i.e. low divergence); at distinct time points (average 261.35 s.d. 239.86 days, first quartile 72 days, third quartile 386 days, 3537 comparisons in total), most of the strain distances (76.4%) approached zero (compared to 1% of comparisons for inter-individual differences, Figure 4B).
evidence: This quantifies within-subject strain retention over time.

claim: Mother-infant pairs showed sporadic vertical transmission of R. bromii (~33.3%).
source: Mother-infant pairs showed a similar dynamic (Figure 4B), with sporadic vertical transmission (~33.3%) (Ferretti et al., 2018; Korpela et al., 2018; Yassour et al., 2018) mixed with strain loss, replacement, and acquisition from other environmental or human sources (Korpela et al., 2018).
evidence: This quantifies the rate of vertical transmission.

claim: PanPhlAn 3 revealed the presence of 6151 UniRef90 pangenes across 2679 R. bromii samples.
source: Using eight R. bromii reference genomes, PanPhlAn 3 revealed the presence of 6151 UniRef90 pangenes across 2679 samples with sufficient depth to permit confident strain-specific gene repertoire reconstruction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This quantifies the pangenome content detected.

claim: R. bromii Cluster 1 showed 797 UniRef90 families specific to it (Fisher's exact test, FDR q < 0.05).
source: This mirrored the genetic divergence of R. bromii Clusters 1 and 2, while also highlighting a range of functional differences annotatable to genes unique to the two clusters: Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 showed a total of 797 and 601 UniRef90 families specific to them (Fisher's exact test, FDR q < 0.05).
evidence: This quantifies the clade-specific gene content.

claim: R. bromii Cluster 2 showed 601 UniRef90 families specific to it (Fisher's exact test, FDR q < 0.05).
source: This mirrored the genetic divergence of R. bromii Clusters 1 and 2, while also highlighting a range of functional differences annotatable to genes unique to the two clusters: Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 showed a total of 797 and 601 UniRef90 families specific to them (Fisher's exact test, FDR q < 0.05).
evidence: This quantifies the clade-specific gene content.

claim: StrainPhlAn 3 and PanPhlAn 3 genetic and genomic distances are correlated (Pearson's r = 0.632, p<2.2e-16).
source: StrainPhlan 3 and PanPhlAn 3 can thus be combined with PhyloPhlAn 3 (Asnicar et al., 2020) and HUMAnN 3 to provide multiple, complementary, culture-independent means to investigate the strain-level diversity of taxa in the microbiome, from new data or by re-using thousands of publicly available metagenomes. It is notable that these approaches tend to be consistent with each other (e.g. for R. bromii, Pearson's r = 0.632, p<2.2e-16, Figure 4D), while providing different benefits and drawbacks: PanPhlAn used with HUMAnN input is computationally efficient, used from whole pangenomes has higher sensitivity, and StrainPhlAn tends to have higher specificity.
evidence: This quantifies the correlation between different strain profiling approaches.

claim: All components of bioBakery 3 are available as open-source implementations at http://segatalab.cibio.unitn.it/tools/biobakery and http://huttenhower.sph.harvard.edu/biobakery.
source: All components are available as open-source implementations with documentation, source code, and workflows enabling provenance, reproducibility, and local or cloud deployment at http://segatalab.cibio.unitn.it/tools/biobakery and http://huttenhower.sph.harvard.edu/biobakery.
evidence: This states the availability of the software.
